title: Friends, Tomorrow, and the Care of the Flock
summary: This chapter gathers sayings on humility about the future, on the value of honest friends and honest rebuke, on neighbors and family, on prudence, and on the restless human appetite. It closes with a short poem urging the reader to know the condition of his flocks and herds, because wealth and even crowns do not last, while faithful work provides for a household.
story: Chapter 27 continues the collection copied by Hezekiah's scribes. After the portraits of fools and slackers in chapter 26, this chapter turns to relationships: friends, neighbors, brothers, and a father's hopes for his son. It is one of the warmest chapters in Proverbs, full of sayings about friendship that have become part of ordinary speech. It ends differently from most chapters, with a sustained piece of advice about tending livestock, a reminder that wisdom concerns the practical economy of a household as much as its relationships.
historical:
Like the rest of chapters 25 to 29, these sayings are attributed to Solomon and were copied in the reign of Hezekiah, around 715 to 686 BC. The chapter reflects a society of small farmers and herders, merchants, and moneylenders. Verse 13, almost identical to 20:16, deals with the practice of guaranteeing someone else's loan, which Proverbs repeatedly warns against. The law of Moses permitted a lender to take a cloak as a pledge but required it to be returned by nightfall so the poor man could sleep in it (Exodus 22:26-27); this proverb advises holding firmly to security when the borrower's guarantor has been reckless.

The closing poem (verses 23 to 27) describes a pastoral economy in which flocks provided wool for clothing, goats could be sold to buy land, and goats' milk fed the family and its servants. This was the backbone of life in the hill country of Judah.
cultural:
Friendship in the ancient world included obligations of loyalty that often extended across generations. Verse 10 warns against abandoning your father's friend, a relationship inherited like property, and notes that in a time of trouble a neighbor who is near can do more than a brother who is far away. Hospitality and neighborliness were matters of survival in small communities without police or social services.

Sheol and Abaddon (verse 20) are names for the realm of the dead; Abaddon means destruction. Both are pictured as never full, always ready to take in more. The crucible and furnace of verse 21 come from the metalworker's shop, where silver and gold were refined by heat. The mortar and pestle of verse 22 were the household tools used to pound grain; even such pounding cannot separate a fool from his folly.
literary: The chapter mixes the book's standard two-line sayings with a few longer units. Many sayings work by comparison (verses 8, 15-16, 17, 19, 21). Several use the better-than form (verses 5 and 10), which ranks two goods or two evils. The chapter shows a loose clustering: verses 1 and 2 on boasting and praise, verses 5 to 10 on friendship, verses 15 and 16 on a contentious wife, and the closing poem of verses 23 to 27, which is the most extended unit in chapters 25 to 29. That poem uses the language of a shepherd, but it follows a line about the impermanence of crowns, so many readers hear it as advice for rulers as well as herders.

outline.t: Tomorrow, praise, and the weight of a fool's provocation
A son's wisdom, prudence, and trying people
Sharpening, faithfulness, the heart, and testing
Know the condition of your flocks

doctrines.note: “You do not know what a day may bring” (verse 1). The future belongs to God, not to our planning, and the proper response is humility, not anxiety.

Verse 19 says the heart reflects the true man, and verse 20 that human eyes are never satisfied. The chapter portrays people as defined by their inner life and marked by a restless desire that nothing created can fill.
The sayings on friendship (verses 5, 6, 9, 17) describe a community where people tell each other the truth and sharpen one another. Christians have long applied them to life together in the church.

words.note: Ahav, to love, used here as a participle meaning friend or lover. Verse 6 says the wounds of a friend are faithful. A true friend's love is shown partly by his willingness to wound with truth, while an enemy offers pleasant kisses that deceive.

Aman, to be faithful or firm, the root behind amen and the Hebrew words for faithfulness and truth. The wounds of a friend are neeman, faithful, that is, trustworthy and reliable. The word links honesty with loyalty.

Chadad, to sharpen. Verse 17 uses the verb twice: as iron sharpens iron, so one man sharpens another. The image suggests friction that improves both, though some interpreters note that sharpening can also describe a sharp, even contentious, exchange.

Sava, to be satisfied or full. Verse 20 uses it twice: Sheol and Abaddon are never satisfied, and neither are human eyes. The verse diagnoses a restless appetite that no amount of seeing or having can fill.

christ: James 4:13-16 develops verse 1 almost directly, warning those who say they will go to a city and make money that they do not know what tomorrow will bring, and that their life is a mist. Jesus' parable of the rich fool, who plans bigger barns and dies that night, makes the same point. The chapter's picture of a friend whose wounds are faithful finds its fullest expression in Jesus, who told his disciples hard truths because he loved them and who called them friends. And the closing poem about knowing the condition of one's flocks is part of the Bible's larger picture of good shepherding, which Jesus takes up when he calls himself the good shepherd who knows his sheep. The connection is thematic, not a prediction.
questions: Verse 6 says the wounds of a friend are faithful. Who in your life has loved you enough to tell you something hard, and how did you respond?
“As iron sharpens iron, so one man sharpens another.” Who sharpens you, and whom are you sharpening?
Verses 23 to 27 urge careful attention to what has been entrusted to you. What flock, whether people, work, or resources, do you need to know better?
